claim: HCC represents the sixth most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related death.
source: HCC represents the sixth most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related death (Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sung et al., 2021

claim: In 2020, the combination of Atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) and Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) became the first-line FDA-approved therapy for advanced HCC.
source: In 2020, the combination of Atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) and Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) became the first-line FDA-approved therapy for advanced HCC (Finn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finn et al., 2020

claim: β-catenin-mutated HCC are devoid of immune infiltrates and are resistant to immunotherapy.
source: Despite this therapeutic advance, several studies emphasized that ß-catenin-mutated HCC are devoid of immune infiltrates and are resistant to immunotherapy (Akasu et al., 2021; Pinyol et al., 2019; Ruiz de Galarreta et al., 2019; Sia et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies by Akasu et al., 2021; Pinyol et al., 2019; Ruiz de Galarreta et al., 2019; Sia et al., 2017

claim: CTNNB1 gene mutations are found in 30–40% of HCC and trigger uncontrolled transcriptional activity.
source: CTNNB1 gene mutations are found in 30–40% of HCC and trigger uncontrolled transcriptional activity (de La Coste et al., 1998; Rebouissou et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to de La Coste et al., 1998; Rebouissou et al., 2016

claim: Silencing of mutated β-catenin in HepG2 cells leads to upregulation of genes associated with exosomes.
source: Gene ontology analysis (FunRich) performed on upregulated genes showed that mutated ß-catenin silencing enhanced significantly the expression of genes linked to specific cellular components, including exosomes (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1b

claim: Silencing of mutated β-catenin in HepG2 cells increases expression of RAB27A and SDC4 genes.
source: Moreover, silencing of the mutated ß-catenin led to the overexpression of 17 genes associated with exosome biogenesis, such as RAB27A and SDC4 (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1c

claim: Proteomic analysis of HepG2 cells with silenced mutated β-catenin shows exosomes as the main cellular component with up-regulated proteins.
source: Similarly, proteomic analysis of HepG2 KD cells revealed exosomes as the main cellular component displaying up-regulated proteins upon mutated ß-catenin silencing (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis shown in Figure 1d-e

claim: Stable depletion of mutated β-catenin in HepG2 cells reduces protein expression by 62% for mutated β-catenin and by 42% for CyclinD1.
source: In HepG2 cells, this strategy reduced protein expression by 62% for mutated ß-catenin and by 42% for CyclinD1, a ß-catenin-positive transcriptional target (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2a

claim: Nanoparticle-tracking analysis reveals that depleting mutated β-catenin increases the number of secreted particles.
source: Nanoparticle-tracking analysis (NTA) revealed that depleting mutated ß-catenin using either siRNA or shRNA increased the number of secreted particles (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by NTA data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The particle mean size (100–150 nm) is consistent with the size of typical small EVs, such as exosomes.
source: The particle mean size (100–150 nm), unaltered by either approach, was consistent with the size of typical small EVs, such as exosomes (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by NTA data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Mutated β-catenin depletion in HepG2 cells significantly increases the number of fusion events associated with secreted exosomes.
source: We found that mutated ß-catenin depletion in HepG2 cells significantly increased the number of fusion events associated with secreted exosomes (Figure 2c, Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2c and Videos 1 and 2

claim: Western-blot analysis of isolated EVs confirms the expression of the CD63 exosomal marker.
source: First, western-blot analysis of isolated EVs confirmed the expression of the CD63 exosomal marker.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis mentioned in the text

claim: CD63 expression increases after mutated β-catenin depletion, suggesting an overall increase in the exosomal fraction.
source: It is noteworthy that we observed an increase in CD63 expression after mutated ß-catenin depletion, suggesting an overall increase in the exosomal fraction (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2e

claim: HepG2-derived EVs have the morphology (flat cup-shaped) and size (50–150 nm) of typical exosomes.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), we demonstrated that HepG2-derived EVs have the morphology (flat cup-shaped) and size (50–150 nm) of typical exosomes (Yang et al., 2019; Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 5, and citation to Yang et al., 2019

claim: Removal of mutated β-catenin results in a higher number of MVBs per cell and an increase in their diameter.
source: We observed a higher number of MVBs per cell and an increase in their diameter upon removal of mutated ß-catenin (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2g

claim: Mutated β-catenin represses exosome secretion.
source: Taken together these results highlight that mutated ß-catenin represses exosome secretion.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript

claim: Stable mutated β-catenin depletion in HepG2 cells increases SDC4 and RAB27A gene expression.
source: In HepG2 cells, we confirmed that transient (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and stable (Figure 3a–b) mutated ß-catenin depletion increased gene and protein expression of both SDC4 and RAB27A.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 3a-b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Mutated β-catenin depletion increases expression of Syndecan-4 and Rab27a by immunofluorescence.
source: However, we were able to confirm the increased expression of Syndecan-4 and Rab27a by immunofluorescence (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c-d

claim: There are positive correlations between SDC4 and RAB27A with ARG1 (β-catenin-negative target) in liver cancer cell lines.
source: We analyzed SDC4, RAB27A, ARG1, and AXIN2 basal mRNA expression in five different liver cancer cell lines, each with a different CTNNB1 mutational status, and identified positive correlations between SDC4 and RAB27A with ARG1 (ß-catenin-negative target) and negative correlations between SDC4 and RAB27A with AXIN2 (ß-catenin-positive target) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: There are negative correlations between SDC4 and RAB27A with AXIN2 (β-catenin-positive target) in liver cancer cell lines.
source: We analyzed SDC4, RAB27A, ARG1, and AXIN2 basal mRNA expression in five different liver cancer cell lines, each with a different CTNNB1 mutational status, and identified positive correlations between SDC4 and RAB27A with ARG1 (ß-catenin-negative target) and negative correlations between SDC4 and RAB27A with AXIN2 (ß-catenin-positive target) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: There is a negative correlation between β-catenin and Rab27a protein expression in liver cancer cell lines.
source: Upon analyzing the basal expression of Rab27a protein in these five cell lines, we identified a negative correlation between ß-catenin and Rab27a expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: β-catenin depletion increases SDC4 and RAB27A gene expression and Rab27a protein expression in Huh6 and SNU398 cells.
source: As in HepG2 cells, ß-catenin depletion also increased SDC4 and RAB27A gene expression and Rab27a protein expression in Huh6 and SNU398 cells treated with doxycycline (Figure 3e–h).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 3e-h

claim: CHIR99021 treatment increases β-catenin protein expression (2.37-fold) in Huh7 cells.
source: This CHIR99021 treatment increased ß-catenin protein expression (2.37-fold) (Figure 3i) and induced its translocation into the nucleus in Huh7 cells (Figure 3j) where concomitant deregulation of ß-catenin transcriptional targets was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3i

claim: CHIR99021 treatment induces β-catenin translocation into the nucleus in Huh7 cells.
source: This CHIR99021 treatment increased ß-catenin protein expression (2.37-fold) (Figure 3i) and induced its translocation into the nucleus in Huh7 cells (Figure 3j) where concomitant deregulation of ß-catenin transcriptional targets was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3j

claim: CHIR99021 treatment decreases SDC4 and RAB27A gene expression, and Rab27a protein level in Huh7 cells.
source: Consistent with our earlier data using HepG2 cells, CHIR99021 treatment decreased SDC4 and RAB27A gene expression, and Rab27a protein level in Huh7 cells (Figure 3k–l).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 3k-l

claim: CHIR99021 treatment significantly decreases the number of fusion events in Huh7 cells.
source: Then, we used TIRF microscopy to analyze exosomal release in living Huh7 cells expressing CD63-pHluorin. We found that CHIR99021 treatment significantly decreased the number of fusion events in Huh7 cells (Figure 3m, Video 3 and Video 4).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3m and Videos 3 and 4

claim: β-catenin mutation/activation represses the expression of syndecan-4 and Rab27A in association with repression of exosomal secretion.
source: All together, these results revealed that ß-catenin mutation/activation represses the expression of syndecan-4 and Rab27A, two proteins involved in exosome biogenesis, in association with repression of exosomal secretion.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript

claim: CHIR99021 treatment decreases PBMC infiltration and increases tumor cell survival in Huh7 spheroids.
source: We observed a decrease in PBMC infiltration and an increase in tumor cell survival in Huh7 cells were treated with CHIR9901 compared to the results seen in the control condition (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4c

claim: Depletion of mutated β-catenin enhances PBMC infiltration in HepG2 spheroids associated with a decrease in tumor cell survival.
source: Next, we showed that the depletion of mutated ß-catenin protein enhanced PBMC infiltration in HepG2 cells associated with a decrease in tumor cell survival (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4d

claim: Rab27a depletion decreases PBMC infiltration associated with an increase of tumor cell survival in HepG2 spheroids depleted of mutated β-catenin.
source: Furthermore, depletion of Rab27a decreased PBMC infiltration associated with an increase of tumor cell survival (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Exosomes play a determinant role in immune cell infiltration.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest a determinant role for exosomes in immune cell infiltration.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results on Rab27a depletion and PBMC infiltration

claim: SDC4 and RAB27A gene expressions are significantly reduced in CTNNB1-mutated HCCs compared to non-mutated tumors in the TCGA cohort.
source: In both sets of data, we showed that SDC4 and RAB27A gene expressions were significantly reduced in CTNNB1-mutated HCCs compared to non-mutated tumors (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data analysis shown in Figure 5a-b

claim: SDC4 and RAB27A gene expressions are significantly reduced in CTNNB1-mutated HCCs compared to non-mutated tumors in the Boyault et al. cohort.
source: In both sets of data, we showed that SDC4 and RAB27A gene expressions were significantly reduced in CTNNB1-mutated HCCs compared to non-mutated tumors (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data analysis shown in Figure 5a-b

claim: RAB27A and SDC4 gene expression are positively correlated with the expression of ARG1 and PCK1 (β-catenin-negative targets) in HCC patient cohorts.
source: Furthermore, Pearson's correlation analysis of these two cohorts revealed that RAB27A and SDC4 gene expression were positively correlated with the expression of ARG1 and PCK1 (ß-catenin-negative targets) (Benhamouche et al., 2006) and negatively correlated with the expression of GLUL, CCND1, AXIN2, LGR5, FAT1, and BMP4 (ß-catenin-positive targets) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Pearson's correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Benhamouche et al., 2006

claim: RAB27A and SDC4 gene expression are negatively correlated with the expression of GLUL, CCND1, AXIN2, LGR5, FAT1, and BMP4 (β-catenin-positive targets) in HCC patient cohorts.
source: Furthermore, Pearson's correlation analysis of these two cohorts revealed that RAB27A and SDC4 gene expression were positively correlated with the expression of ARG1 and PCK1 (ß-catenin-negative targets) (Benhamouche et al., 2006) and negatively correlated with the expression of GLUL, CCND1, AXIN2, LGR5, FAT1, and BMP4 (ß-catenin-positive targets) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Pearson's correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Tumors strongly positive for glutamine synthetase are correlated with low levels of Rab27a protein expression.
source: We found that tumors strongly positive for glutamine synthetase (a well-known ß-catenin-positive target in the liver Cadoret et al., 2002), were correlated with low levels of Rab27a protein expression (Figure 5c), supporting the link between ß-catenin activation and regulation of exosomal secretion through a decrease in Rab27a expression.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5c and citation to Cadoret et al., 2002

claim: Oncogenic β-catenin plays a key role in exosome biogenesis.
source: Taken together, our results provide the first evidence that oncogenic ß-catenin plays a key role in exosome biogenesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from all experimental results presented in the manuscript

claim: Activation of β-catenin promotes a decrease in immune cell infiltration through a defect in exosome secretion.
source: Then, we demonstrated in 3D spheroid models that activation of β-catenin promotes a decrease in immune cell infiltration through a defect in exosome secretion.
evidence: Supported by 3D spheroid experiments with PBMC infiltration assays

claim: HCC is the most frequent form of primary liver adult cancer (80% of cases).
source: HCC is the most frequent form of primary liver adult cancer (80% of cases).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about HCC

claim: β-catenin is a main oncogene, mutated in various cancers, such as melanoma and liver, endometrial, and colorectal cancers.
source: ß-catenin, encoded by the CTNNB1 gene, is a main oncogene, mutated in various cancers, such as melanoma and liver, endometrial, and colorectal cancers (Kim and Jeong, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Jeong, 2019

claim: β-catenin-mutated tumors share specific features, prominent among them a microenvironment devoid of immune infiltrates.
source: These ß-catenin-mutated tumors share specific features, prominent among them a microenvironment devoid of immune infiltrates.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about β-catenin-mutated tumors

claim: Most β-catenin-mutated tumors remain resistant to immunotherapy.
source: Thus, despite of a therapeutic revolution for cancer treatment, with the emergence of immunotherapy and more particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD1, anti-PD-L1), most of the ß-catenin-mutated tumors remain resistant to immunotherapy (Yaguchi et al., 2012; Spranger et al., 2015; Du et al., 2020; Cen et al., 2021; Rotman et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies by Yaguchi et al., 2012; Spranger et al., 2015; Du et al., 2020; Cen et al., 2021; Rotman et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020

claim: In melanoma and HCC, a decrease in CCL4 and CCL5 leads to a defective recruitment of dendritic cells and consequently impaired T-cell activity and immune escape.
source: In melanoma and HCC, a decrease in CCL4 and CCL5, leads to a defective recruitment of dendritic cells and consequently impaired T-cell activity and immune escape (Ruiz de Galarreta et al., 2019; Spranger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ruiz de Galarreta et al., 2019; Spranger et al., 2015

claim: Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) are important actors in tumor microenvironment communication.
source: Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly described as important actors in tumor microenvironment communication (van Niel et al., 2018); but no studies explored their role in the immune escape and immunotherapy resistance of ß-catenin-mutated tumors.
evidence: Supported by citation to van Niel et al., 2018

claim: Microvesicles (50–1000 nm) correspond to EVs directly secreted from the plasma membrane.
source: Microvesicles (50–1000 nm) correspond to EVs directly secreted from the plasma membrane (PM).
evidence: Definition of microvesicles based on established knowledge

claim: Exosomes (50–150 nm) are released from an endosomal compartment, the multivesicular body (MVB), by its fusion with the cell surface.
source: By contrast, exosomes (50–150 nm) are released from an endosomal compartment, the multivesicular body (MVB), by its fusion with the cell surface (van Niel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Niel et al., 2018

claim: Syndecan-4 is involved in the endosomal membrane budding.
source: Among the actors implicated in exosome biogenesis and secretion, syndecan-4, involved in the endosomal membrane budding (Baietti et al., 2012) and Rab27a, which promotes the docking of MVB to the PM, play key roles in exosome release (Ostrowski et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baietti et al., 2012

claim: Rab27a promotes the docking of MVB to the PM and plays a key role in exosome release.
source: Among the actors implicated in exosome biogenesis and secretion, syndecan-4, involved in the endosomal membrane budding (Baietti et al., 2012) and Rab27a, which promotes the docking of MVB to the PM, play key roles in exosome release (Ostrowski et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ostrowski et al., 2010

claim: EVs can regulate tumor growth, angiogenesis, invasion, and infiltration of immune cells into the tumor.
source: As important mediators of cell-to-cell communication, EVs can regulate tumor growth, angiogenesis, invasion, and infiltration of immune cells into the tumor (Tkach and Théry, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tkach and Théry, 2016

claim: EVs derived from tumor cells can modulate epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, intrahepatic metastasis, and tumor immunity in HCC.
source: In the context of HCC, it was reported that EVs derived from tumor cells can modulate epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, intrahepatic metastasis, and tumor immunity (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021

claim: Mutated β-catenin represses syndecan-4 and Rab27a expression, thus altering exosomal secretion from HCC cells, in turn leading to a defective recruitment of immune cells in tumors.
source: We demonstrated that mutated ß-catenin represses syndecan-4 and Rab27a expression, thus altering exosomal secretion from HCC cells, in turn leading to a defective recruitment of immune cells in tumors.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all experimental results presented in the manuscript

claim: The transcriptional analysis of HepG2 KD cells revealed that the expression of 1973 genes is modulated upon mutated β-catenin silencing.
source: The transcriptional analysis of HepG2 KD cells revealed that the expression of 1973 genes (log2(Fold-change) >0.5 and<−0.5) is modulated upon mutated ß-catenin silencing (Gest et al., 2023; Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1a and citation to Gest et al., 2023

claim: Genes from the Rab (RAB8B, RAB11A, RAB11B, RAB17, RAB27A), Vamp (VAMP2, VAMP5, VAMP8) and Vps (VPS4A, VPS4B, VPS16, VPS28) families are upregulated upon removal of the oncogenic β-catenin in HepG2 cells.
source: We indeed found that genes from the Rab (RAB8B, RAB11A, RAB11B, RAB17, RAB27A), Vamp (VAMP2, VAMP5, VAMP8) and Vps (VPS4A, VPS4B, VPS16, VPS28) families were upregulated upon removal of the oncogenic ß-catenin in HepG2 cells.
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic analysis results

claim: Several trafficking steps could be impaired along the EV secretion pathway, including MVB biogenesis with the Vps, the transport and docking with the Rab, and the final step of membrane fusion with the Vamp.
source: Therefore, several trafficking steps could be impaired along the EV secretion pathway, the MVB biogenesis with the Vps, the transport and docking with the Rab, and the final step of membrane fusion with the Vamp (van Niel et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on gene expression data and citation to van Niel et al., 2018

claim: The way RAB27A and SDC4 gene expression is repressed by β-catenin remains to be explored.
source: The way RAB27A and SDC4 gene expression is repressed by ß-catenin remains to be explored.
evidence: Statement acknowledging a gap in current understanding

claim: The transcription repressor ATF3 induced by the Wnt/β-catenin pathway has been associated with CCL4 repression in melanoma.
source: In melanoma, the transcription repressor ATF3 induced by the Wnt/ß-catenin pathway has been associated with CCL4 repression (Spranger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spranger et al., 2015

claim: Analysis of SDC4 and RAB27A promoter sequences revealed the presence of consensus sequences of Lef1, Tcf4, and Atf3 binding.
source: Analysis of SDC4 and RAB27A promoter sequences revealed the presence of consensus sequences of Lef1, Tcf4, and Atf3 binding (data not shown), suggesting that these newly identified target genes could be regulated at the transcriptional level by transcription factors known to associate with ß-catenin.
evidence: Supported by promoter sequence analysis (data not shown)

claim: SDC4 was found to be a negative Tcf4 target gene in HCC mouse models.
source: In this line, SDC4 was found to be a negative Tcf4 target gene in HCC mouse models (Gougelet et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gougelet et al., 2014

claim: Mutated β-catenin promotes a decrease of immune cell infiltration in micro-tumors through a decrease in exosome secretion.
source: Using siRNA depletion of Rab27a, we showed that mutated ß-catenin promotes a decrease of immune cell infiltration in micro-tumors through a decrease in exosome secretion.
evidence: Supported by experimental results using siRNA depletion of Rab27a in spheroid models

claim: The small GTPase Rab27a has been implicated in several cancer progression mechanisms such as metastasis, cell invasion, or migration.
source: The small GTPase Rab27a has been implicated in several cancer progression mechanisms such as metastasis, cell invasion, or migration (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2018

claim: In mammary carcinoma cells, the decrease of exosome secretion by Rab27a inhibition resulted in a diminution of primary tumor growth and lung metastatic dissemination.
source: In mammary carcinoma cells, the decrease of exosome secretion by Rab27a inhibition resulted in a diminution of primary tumor growth and lung metastatic dissemination (Bobrie et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bobrie et al., 2012

claim: shRNA knockdown of Rab27a in a prostate cancer model revealed a dominant immunosuppressive role for EVs during antigen cross-presentation.
source: However, shRNA knockdown of Rab27a in a prostate cancer model revealed a dominant immunosuppressive role for EVs during antigen cross-presentation (Salimu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Salimu et al., 2017

claim: Rab27a-induced exosomal secretion could be a 'double-edged sword' in tumor progression.
source: These data are inconsistent with our own, meaning so it seems that Rab27a-induced exosomal secretion could be a 'double-edged sword' in tumor progression.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of different study results

claim: EVs are known to contain heterogeneous cargos that can play a critical role in immunomodulation.
source: This could be due to the content of EVs. In fact, EVs are known to contain heterogeneous cargos that can play a critical role in immunomodulation (Marar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marar et al., 2021

claim: The main immunosuppressive cytokine TGF-β expressed by tumoral-derived EVs has been identified in Natural Killer cell function suppression.
source: For example, the main immunosuppressive cytokine TGF-ß expressed by tumoral-derived EVs has been identified in Natural Killer cell function suppression (Berchem et al., 2016; Viel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berchem et al., 2016; Viel et al., 2016

claim: MiR-103a and Let-7a in tumor EVs promote M2-like polarization in lung and melanoma cancers.
source: MiR-103a and Let-7a in tumor EVs promote M2-like polarization in lung and melanoma cancers (Hsu et al., 2018; Park et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hsu et al., 2018; Park et al., 2019

claim: Immunomodulatory proteins such as CSF-1, CCL2, FTH, FTL, and TGF-β chemokines have been identified in tumor exosomes.
source: Interestingly, immunomodulatory proteins such as CSF-1, CCL2, FTH, FTL, and TGF-β chemokines have been identified in tumor exosomes (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2019

claim: The content of β-catenin-regulated EVs remains to be explored to fully understand their function in the immunomodulation of the tumor microenvironment.
source: The content of ß-catenin-regulated EVs remains to be explored to fully understand their function in the immunomodulation of the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: Statement acknowledging a gap in current understanding

claim: This study is the first description of the oncogenic β-catenin as a key regulator of the exosome machinery.
source: In conclusion, this study is the first description of the oncogenic ß-catenin as a key regulator of the exosome machinery.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's main finding

claim: Exosomes could be a promising biomarker for β-catenin-mutated tumors.
source: Our data indicate that exosomes could be a promising biomarker and that restoring the tumor exosomal secretion of ß-catenin-mutated tumors may increase the communication between tumor and immune cells, and as a result, turn cold tumors hot.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on study findings

claim: Restoring the tumor exosomal secretion of β-catenin-mutated tumors may increase the communication between tumor and immune cells, and as a result, turn cold tumors hot.
source: Our data indicate that exosomes could be a promising biomarker and that restoring the tumor exosomal secretion of ß-catenin-mutated tumors may increase the communication between tumor and immune cells, and as a result, turn cold tumors hot.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on study findings

claim: Given that β-catenin is also mutated in melanoma, endometrial, and colorectal cancers, these new findings may have a broader significance.
source: Given that ß-catenin is also mutated in melanoma, endometrial, and colorectal cancers, these new findings may have a broader significance.
evidence: Inference about broader implications based on study findings

claim: CD63 is a well-known exosome surface marker.
source: The tetraspanin CD63 is a well-known exosome surface marker (Jeppesen et al., 2019; Kowal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jeppesen et al., 2019; Kowal et al., 2016

claim: Both the WT and the mutated forms of the β-catenin protein are found in HepG2-derived EVs.
source: Moreover, the WT and the mutated forms of the ß-catenin protein were also found in HepG2-derived EVs, and the expression of mutated ß-catenin was decreased relative to the cells of origin (Figure 2e).

claim: The expression of mutated β-catenin in HepG2-derived EVs is decreased relative to the cells of origin.
source: Moreover, the WT and the mutated forms of the ß-catenin protein were also found in HepG2-derived EVs, and the expression of mutated ß-catenin was decreased relative to the cells of origin (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Mutated β-catenin depletion in HepG2 cells increases the number and size of bile canaliculi, a feature of more differentiated cells.
source: Also, as previously described with the siRNA strategy (Gest et al., 2023), after mutated ß-catenin depletion in HepG2 cells, we observed an increase in the number and size of bile canaliculi (BC), feature of more differentiated cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citation to Gest et al., 2023

claim: CHIR99021 treatment increases β-catenin and decreases Rab27a protein expression in Huh7 spheroids with no impact on cell viability.
source: Of note, we confirmed that CHIR99021 increased ß-catenin and decreased Rab27a protein expression in Huh7 spheroids with no impact on the cell viability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot and viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Mutated β-catenin protein is correctly depleted in HepG2 spheroids, with an increase in Rab27a protein expression and no impact on cell viability.
source: We verified that mutated ß-catenin protein was correctly depleted in HepG2 spheroids, with an increase in Rab27a protein expression and no impact on cell viability (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by western blot and viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Rab27a depletion decreases the number of secreted particles without any effect on cell viability in HepG2 shβcat MUT spheroids.
source: Rab27a depletion decreased the number of secreted particles without any effect on cell viability in HepG2 shßcat MUT spheroids (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by NTA and viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Inducible shRNA strategy with doxycycline reduces β-catenin protein expression by 63% in Huh6 cells and 49% in SNU398 cells.
source: In the two liver cancer cell lines bearing a ß-catenin point mutation (Huh6 and SNU398 cells), inducible shRNA strategy with doxycycline reduced ß-catenin protein expression by 63% and 49%, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: β-catenin depletion decreases CCND1 and AXIN2 mRNA expression and increases ARG1 mRNA expression in Huh6 and SNU398 cells.
source: Associated with that reduction in ß-catenin protein expression we observed a decrease in CCND1 and AXIN2 mRNA expression and an increase in ARG1 mRNA expression in both cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5

claim: CHIR99021 treatment causes concomitant deregulation of β-catenin transcriptional targets in Huh7 cells.
source: This CHIR99021 treatment increased ß-catenin protein expression (2.37-fold) (Figure 3i) and induced its translocation into the nucleus in Huh7 cells (Figure 3j) where concomitant deregulation of ß-catenin transcriptional targets was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6
